concept.title: Journey Definition (Single Trip vs Multiple Consecutive trips)
concept.shortdesc: You can define journeys as either a single trip or consecutive trips with pauses.

dd.p: Select A single trip (default) to define a journey as "When a vehicle starts moving until it stops with ignition turned off (or idles for 3 min 20 sec)".
Select Chained consecutive trips to define a journey as combined, consecutive trips, with pauses in work (e.g. breaks).

The concept of Trip Chaining is unique to , as is a primary source of data and has the ability to follow vehicles along an entire journey. Particularly for heavy-duty or long haul vehicles, a standard definition for a trip may not be useful. In this case, a trip chaining factor, which is the minimum stop duration threshold, can be defined to string together trips to comprise a journey from origin to destination. You can do this by inputting a number of minutes to Chain consecutive trips together by ignoring stops under: field.Trip chaining threshold field
To determine how trip chaining will combine certain trips into a single journey, select the appropriate parameters according to their description:

entry.p: Set the minimum stop duration (in minutes) to chain consecutive trips into a single journey. Stops shorter than this threshold are ignored, linking the surrounding trips together. Useful to see, for example, the complete journey of a long-haul truck that makes brief stops. This can help you analyze full door-to-door journeys rather than individual trip segments.

Add journey counts for destination stops on the way to the final destination. Useful to see, for example, if trucks are hitting multiple defined destinations on their way to a final Destination. This can help you understand how goods are moving and stopping along longer journeys. This setting is not considered if the destination is set to passthrough.

Metrics account for trips chained within an Origin. Useful to see, for example, how efficiently trucks move through a warehouse center. This can help you understand if you need additional docks or parking areas.

Include journeys whose stop duration in the initial Origin is shorter than the Trip Chaining Threshold. Useful to see, for example, the total traffic demand for a geography. This can help you plan the road infrastructure to accommodate the right types of volumes.

Metrics account for trips chained within a Destination. Useful to see, for example, how efficiently trucks move through a warehouse center. This can help you understand if you need additional docks or parking areas.

Include journeys whose stop duration in the final Destination is shorter than the Trip Chaining Threshold. Useful to see, for example, the total traffic demand for a geography. This can help you plan the road infrastructure to accommodate the right types of volumes.

note.p: Some parameters depend on others, so you can only select Include Inbound Chaining if you select Chaining Within Origins.
You can also only select Include Outbound Chaining if you select Chaining Within Destinations
